t: LeetCode 2216 - Minimum Deletions to Make Array Beautiful: One Greedy Pass
o: **Understanding the problem.** An array is beautiful when its length is even and, reading it in pairs (positions 0-1, 2-3, ...), the two members of every pair differ. Deleting elements shifts everything left, so what matters is the sequence of survivors. In Example 1 ([1,1,2,3,5]) removing one of the twin 1s yields [1,2,3,5], whose pairs (1,2) and (3,5) differ - one deletion. In Example 2 ([1,1,2,2,3,3]) dropping nums[0] and nums[5] leaves [1,2,2,3] with differing pairs - two deletions. Reframed, we keep the longest survivable sequence in which consecutive kept elements pair up unequally; a single left-to-right greedy achieves this because a conflicting duplicate can always be discarded without regret.
k: Beautiful arrays are exactly sequences whose adjacent pairs (indices 0-1, 2-3, ...) consist of unequal values.
Exchange argument: when the incoming value equals the pending partner, deleting it is never worse than deleting the pending element, so greedy discarding is optimal.
If an odd number of elements survives, the last one forms an unpairable tail and must be deleted too.

a.n: Approach 1: Greedy With an Explicit Kept List
a.i: Maintain the survivor list. Before appending a value, check whether the list currently has odd length (meaning this value would close a pair) and equals the previous survivor; if so, skip it and charge one deletion. Otherwise append. Finally, if the list length is odd, one more deletion trims the dangling tail. Equal-value runs collapse automatically because each run member after the first clashes with the pending partner.
s: Initialize an empty kept list and a deletion counter.
For each x: if len(kept) is odd and kept[-1] == x, increment deletions and skip; otherwise append x.
After the scan, add len(kept) % 2 for a possible trailing deletion.
a.t: O(n) - each element inspected once with O(1) work
a.sp: O(n) - the kept list mirrors the input in the worst case

a.i: The kept list is only ever queried for its length parity and its last element, so two variables - count of kept elements and last kept value - capture all state. Replace the list with those counters and the algorithm keeps identical decisions while dropping auxiliary memory to O(1), a worthwhile refinement to present after the readable version.
s: Track kept (count so far) and prev (last kept value).
For each x: skip and count a deletion if kept is odd and prev == x; otherwise increment kept and set prev = x.
Add kept % 2 at the end for the parity fix.
a.t: O(n) - single pass with constant work per element

w: Open with the explicit-list version for clarity, then compress to the constant-space variant - interviewers reward recognizing that only parity and the last survivor matter. Pitfalls: forgetting the trailing parity deletion (input [7] needs one deletion, since the empty array is the nearest beautiful state); assuming runs of equal values need special casing (the greedy handles [2,2,2] by keeping one and deleting two); and confusing pair alignment - after any deletion, subsequent comparisons use the NEW parity, which the simulation does automatically. Follow-ups: return the lexicographically smallest beautiful result, or allow one swap to reduce deletions.
